title: Futurama: the Planet Express ship's dark matter engines (1999 onward)
hook: The engines don't move the ship; the ship stays where it is and the engines move the universe around it, which is a warp drive described exactly and as a joke.
text: the drive as depicted the planet express ship is defined in one scene of "a clone of my own" (production code 2acv10, first aired 9 april 2000) for the dialogue, for the code and date. standing on the hull, professor farnsworth shows his clone cubert the dark matter engines he invented, which let his ship travel between galaxies in hours. cubert objects that nothing can go faster than the speed of light, and farnsworth agrees: that is why scientists increased the speed of light in 2208 . cubert says that is impossible too. at the end of the episode, having learned that nothing is impossible if you can imagine it, cubert announces that he understands the engines: "the ship stays where it is and the engines move the universe around it" . bender calls this a complete load; the ship then takes off in a slow-motion sequence in which the universe visibly moves past a stationary ship. the fuel is dark matter, established in "love's labours lost in space" (1acv04, 1999): a super-dense substance mined out of the planet vergon 6, each pound of which weighs over ten thousand pounds, valuable as starship fuel, and, as the crew discover, excreted by nibbler . the film bender's game (2008) later renders all dark matter inert when the professor's crystals are destroyed . the engines otherwise do what the plot requires: the ship crosses the galaxy in an episode, reaches other galaxies when a story needs one and runs out of fuel when a story needs that. origin and lineage futurama was

title: Guardians of the Galaxy Vol. 2 (2017): jump points
hook: A galaxy threaded with fixed jump points, a rule that a body should take no more than fifty in a row, and a ship that takes seven hundred.
text: the drive as depicted in the marvel cinematic universe, ships get between stars through jump points: fixed places in space where a ship enters a portal and comes out somewhere far away. the first film (2014) uses them as scene changes. guardians of the galaxy vol. 2 (2017), written and directed by james gunn, is the instalment that states the rules, and it does so twice. the first time is in the opening chase. fleeing the sovereign fleet, quill asks how many jumps it is to the nearest habitable planet, berhert. title: Halo: slipspace and the Shaw-Fujikawa translight engine (2001 onward)
hook: Eleven hidden dimensions entered through a rupture torn by microscopic black holes, crossed at ordinary speed inside a protective field, and left with an error measured in millions of kilometres.
text: the drive as depicted the drive is defined in eric nylund's novel halo: the fall of reach (2001), published alongside the first game, which describes slipstream space as eleven non-visible, infinitesimal dimensions used for faster-than-light travel, with physics that is neither euclidean nor einsteinian (halopedia, "slipstream space", quoting the novel at p. 136; the novel was not reopened). the human drive is the shaw-fujikawa translight engine, named for tobias shaw and wallace fujikawa, who unveiled it in april 2291 according to a memorial plaque in the halo 3 map "orbital" (halopedia, "shaw-fujikawa translight engine"). the mechanism, given in halo: ghosts of onyx (2006, chapter 3), is that particle accelerators make microscopic black holes with lifetimes of nanoseconds and shape them into a coherent rupture between normal space and slipspace before they evaporate; ordinary matter cannot survive raw slipspace, so the drive wraps the ship in a quantum field and, in the words of dr halsey's journal (2009 supplement), squeezes it through the higher dimensions (halopedia, citing both sources). inside slipspace the ship does not accelerate by any new means; ordinary thrusters push it, so a stronger conventional engine means a faster transit (halo: contact harvest, 2007, chapter 1) . human jumps early in the war took weeks to months, at roughly 2.6 light years a day, and missed their targets by millions of kilometres; covenant drives managed over a thousand light years a day

title: The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy: the Infinite Improbability Drive and bistromathics
hook: Douglas Adams's starship drives, from the 1978 radio series and 1979 novel onward: a ship that is everywhere at once because that is very unlikely, and a later one steered by restaurant arithmetic.

title: Homeworld: hyperspace cores and the Far Jumpers
hook: Relic's 1999 strategy game hangs an exodus on a hyperspace core dug out of the desert; its 2003 sequel reveals the core as one of three, each a Far Jumper, and the three together the key to a galaxy's gate network.

title: Weber's Honorverse: hyper bands and Warshawski sails (1993 onward)
hook: Hyperspace as a stack of bands, each with a bigger multiplier and worse weather, sailed on gravity waves by ships that lose most of their speed on the way in.

title: Hyperion: the farcasters (Simmons 1989)
hook: Doorways between worlds that anyone can step through and nobody understands, and the reveal that the people who gave them away were living inside them.
text: the drive as depicted dan simmons's hyperion (doubleday, 1989) and the fall of hyperion (doubleday, march 1990) give the hegemony of man two ways to cross interstellar space and treat them very differently . the farcaster is a portal: a doorway, a room or a river through which a person or a boat passes from one world to another instantly, and the hundreds of worlds joined by farcasters are the worldweb, with houses whose rooms are on different planets and a river that runs through a dozen . farcaster technology was given to humanity by the technocore, the society of artificial intelligences that seceded from human control, and no human understands how it works; the novels describe farcaster portals as singularity spheres that bend spacetime to join distant places, and leave it there . the other way is the hawking drive, a human invention that carries ships faster than light between stars but at a cost the novels keep exactly: time-debt, the years that pass in the web while a ship is in transit . worlds off the web, such as hyperion, are reached only by hawking drive, and the consul's tale in the first novel is built on it: merin aspic makes repeated voyages to maui-covenant and his lover siri ages decades between each, until on his last return she is dead of old age . the fatline, a tachyon-burst communicator, carries messages between worlds without a ship . the second novel is about who owns the doors. the technocore, it emerges, has been the farcasters' landlord and their

title: Interstellar: the wormhole near Saturn (2014)
hook: A wormhole nobody on Earth built, placed by "they", with the clocks at Gargantua done to the equations and a physicist's book to show the working.
text: the drive as depicted interstellar (directed by christopher nolan, released 5 november 2014 in the united states) has one faster-than-light device and it is not on the ship . a wormhole appeared near saturn forty-eight years before the film's present, and nasa, working in secret, has been sending probes and then people through it to a planetary system in another galaxy around the black hole gargantua . the endurance takes two years to reach saturn at ordinary speeds; the wormhole is the whole of the shortcut, and the film is explicit that it did not occur naturally: it was placed by beings the characters call "they", whom the film's ending identifies as humans from the far future acting through higher dimensions . romilly explains the geometry to cooper on the way out with a sheet of paper folded so that a pen pierces two distant points at once, and the exchange ends with the wormhole not being a hole but a sphere, which is what the crew then flies into . the film's second physics set piece is not the wormhole but the clock at gargantua. miller's planet orbits close enough to the black hole that, as romilly puts it, "every hour we spend down there will be maybe... seven years back on earth", and a landing that goes wrong costs the crew twenty-three years of the endurance's time while romilly waits in orbit (line verified via wikiquote, s3 transcription). the film's climax sends cooper into gargantua and into a tesseract, a construction in which time is laid out as a spatial

title: Niven's Known Space: the Outsider hyperdrive and the blind spot (1966 onward)
hook: A drive bought from aliens who never use it, three days to the light year, a window you must not look through, and a rule that a mass nearby will take your ship away for good.
text: the drive as depicted larry niven's known space stories (from 1964; the hyperdrive from 1966) define the drive piecemeal, and the rules are stable enough that niven's fans have kept a concordance. the hyperdrive shunt was sold to humanity by the outsiders, a species of cold, slow-moving beings who trade information and do not use the drive themselves, and the sale ended the first man-kzin war, since the kzinti had no equivalent (wikipedia, "known space", technology and history; the stories "the warriors" (1966) and the man-kzin wars framing from memory). the standard drive, later called quantum i, moves a ship one light year in three days, about 122 times the speed of light (wikipedia; the figure is stated in ringworld, 1970, from memory). a single much faster ship exists: the long shot, a puppeteer-built prototype whose drive covers a light year in about a minute and a quarter, some 420,000 c, flown by beowulf shaeffer to the galactic core in "at the core" (1966) and given the name quantum ii in the ringworld engineers (1980) (wikipedia for the rate; the story and the naming from memory). two rules do most of the work. the first is the mass rule: a ship may only engage the hyperdrive well outside a star's gravity well, and a ship that enters hyperspace, or is in hyperspace, too near a large mass vanishes and is never seen again; the stories treat this as a law of nature, ships carry a mass sensor whose indicator swells toward nearby masses and the pilot's job in hyperspace

title: Le Guin's ansible
hook: The word and the device: Le Guin's instantaneous communicator, coined in 1966 and given its theory in 1974, sitting alongside ships that never beat light.

title: The Lensman inertialess drive (E. E. Smith, 1934 onward)
hook: The Bergenholm switches a ship's inertia off, so any push at all takes it to whatever speed the drag of the interstellar medium allows, and switches it back on with its old velocity intact.
text: the drive as depicted the lensman ships fly "free" or "inert". a generator called the bergenholm neutralises the inertia of the ship and everything in it; with inertia gone, the ship's driving blast is opposed only by the friction of whatever medium it is passing through, and the ship takes up, instantly, the speed at which drive and drag balance. galactic patrol states the rule in an author's footnote in chapter 2: with the neutralisation of inertia there is "no limit whatever to the velocity of inertialess matter", and a free ship takes on the balance velocity instantaneously . in the same chapter the britannia, capable of ten gravities of inert acceleration, crosses space at ninety parsecs an hour, which the narration calls possible only for inertialess matter driven through an almost perfect vacuum . inert matter, the books say repeatedly, cannot even reach the speed of light; free matter has no ceiling but the medium. the drive's second rule is the one that makes it interesting. inertia is switched off, not destroyed, and with it the ship's momentum is stored rather than spent. when the bergenholm is cut the ship "goes inert" and instantly resumes the velocity it had before going free, its "intrinsic velocity", whatever it has done in the meantime. so a ship cannot simply land free on a planet with a different intrinsic velocity and switch on inertia: it would tear away at its old speed. crews must "match intrinsics" by inert manoeuvring before docking, boarding or

title: Super Dimension Fortress Macross (1982): the space fold
hook: An alien fold system in a rebuilt warship, fired once in a panic near the Earth's surface, that takes an island along, lands the ship at Pluto and then is not there any more.
text: the drive as depicted super dimension fortress macross (studio nue and tatsunoko, 36 episodes, broadcast from october 1982) is built on a single early misuse of its drive. the macross itself is an alien warship that crashed on earth in 1999 and was rebuilt over a decade using its own "overtechnology"; its fold system, the mechanism for a space fold, is one of the things nobody has been able to test . episode 3, "space fold" (broadcast 17 october 1982), is where it is used. under attack by the zentradi fleet and having lost his escort carriers, captain global orders a fold to the far side of the moon and, to deceive the enemy, has the ship feint towards its island base and fold from just above it . the fold takes the ship and a sphere of its surroundings, south ataria island and the sea around it, and when the ship comes out it is not behind the moon but in the orbit of pluto . the zentradi commanders watching from orbit are shocked that anyone would fold so close to a planet's surface. global assumes the ship can fold back; the engine room reports that the fold system has disappeared, and the captain lights his pipe and says it is going to be a long trip . the rest of the series is that trip, at ordinary speed, with the island's civilians rebuilding their town inside the ship. that is the entire definition of the drive in the original series. a fold is a jump: the ship vanishes and reappears elsewhere, with no transit shown from inside. it is imprecise, at least when fired

title: Mass Effect: element zero and the FTL drive (BioWare, 2007)
hook: A ship whose mass is dialled down by a dark-energy field can be pushed past light by ordinary thrusters, and pays for it in static charge that must be grounded on a planet.
text: the drive as depicted mass effect defines its drive in the in-game codex, a set of entries unlocked as the player meets each technology and read aloud by a narrator; the entries below are from the first game (2007) and are carried unchanged into the sequels. the codex entry "element zero" says that when the rare material "eezo" is subjected to an electric current it emits a dark energy field that raises or lowers the mass of everything within it, a mass effect used for artificial gravity and construction and most prominently for faster-than-light travel; humanity found refined eezo at a prothean research station on mars . the entry "mass effect fields" adds the sign convention: positive current raises mass, negative current lowers it, and the stronger the current the larger the effect . the entry "ftl drive" is the mechanism. an eezo drive core reduces the mass of the ship, allowing higher acceleration, which the codex says "effectively raises the speed of light within the mass effect field", so that the ship travels fast with negligible relativistic time dilation . a ship still needs conventional thrusters, chemical, fusion, ion or antiproton, because a core alone provides no motive power; the eezo and power required grow exponentially with the mass moved and the degree of lightening, so very massive ships and very high speeds are prohibitively expensive; and if the field collapses at superluminal speed the ship snaps back to sublight and sheds the excess energy as lethal

title: Mass Effect: the mass relays (BioWare 2007 onward)
hook: Corridors of mass-free space between fixed stations, primary relays paired one to one, secondaries reaching any relay in range; the network is a trap and the trap is the plot.
text: the drive as depicted mass effect (bioware, released 20 november 2007) has two faster-than-light systems and documents both in its in-game codex . ships carry drive cores of element zero, which under current emits a field that lowers the mass of everything inside it; the codex entry "ftl drive" says the field effectively raises the speed of light within it and allows high-speed travel "with negligible relativistic time dilation effects" (codex text, read via a fan transcription). that is an l1 move and is scored in the catalogue's mass-effect-element-zero entry. this dossier is the other system. the codex entry "mass relays" describes enormous structures scattered through the galaxy that "create corridors of virtually mass-free space", allowing instantaneous transit between locations that would take years or centuries by drive core . primary relays throw a ship thousands of light years, often between spiral arms, and each is paired with exactly one other primary relay; secondary relays reach only a few hundred light years but are omnidirectional, able to send a ship to any relay within that range . on screen the ship approaches the relay, is caught by its field and is thrown along the corridor in a streak of blue; arrival is at the paired relay and nowhere else . the game's plot is about who built them. the codex attributes the relays to the protheans, an extinct race whose ruins on mars gave humanity the technology . on virmire the reaper sovereign tells shepard the truth:

title: No Man's Sky: the hyperdrive, warp cells and range
hook: Hello Games' 2016 galaxy of eighteen quintillion planets is crossed by a ship-mounted hyperdrive with a range in light-years, a fuel cell per warp and a drive upgrade for each colour of star.
text: the drive as depicted no man's sky was released by hello games on 9 august 2016 and has been rebuilt by free updates since; the drive's rules below are those of the current game, with the launch version noted where it differed . the player begins on a planet with a crashed ship and no hyperdrive, and the opening mission has them build one from a blueprint and fuel it before the first warp out of the starting system . the drive is a ship technology occupying an inventory slot, with a stated range in light-years shown on the galactic map: about a hundred light-years for a bare drive, rising with installed upgrade modules to several thousand for a well-fitted explorer . only systems within range can be selected as a destination; the map draws the reachable ones. fuel is the warp cell, crafted from antimatter and a housing, and one cell is consumed per warp, a fifth of the drive's charge; the drive can be pre-charged with five, and a later item, the warp hypercore, fills it in one . star colour is a gate. a bare hyperdrive reaches only yellow stars; the cadmium drive adds red, the emeril drive green and the indium drive blue, each requiring the previous, so the galaxy's colour classes are a progression the player unlocks . the warp itself is a tunnel of streaked light through which the ship flies for a few seconds before dropping into the destination system near its star, with the option since later updates of being interrupted by a pirate ambush mid-warp . freighters have their

title: Outer Wilds (2019): Nomai warp cores
hook: A video game whose lost civilisation built black-hole-to-white-hole warp towers, noticed that travellers arrive a hundred-thousandth of a second before they leave, and turned that fact into a twenty-two-minute time loop that is the game itself.
text: the drive as depicted outer wilds (mobius digital, published by annapurna interactive, may 2019) is an exploration game set in a toy solar system whose sun explodes twenty-two minutes after the player wakes, after which the player wakes again. its faster-than-light technology belongs to the nomai, a species dead for a very long time, and is learned by reading their wall texts and walking through their machines. the dossier's primary material is those texts, which the game prints in full when a wall is scanned; the wiki citations below reproduce them . a warp core is a pair: a black hole core and a white hole core. whatever is warped enters the black hole and leaves the white hole, and the two can be far apart . the nomai's first use is the white hole station, a platform hanging beside the white hole that is the far end of the natural black hole at the centre of the planet brittle hollow, built to return anyone who fell in . every warp tower is tuned to one astral body and works only during the brief window when that body is directly overhead; poke's welcome text at the station states the rule, and the player learns it by standing on the platform and waiting . on the planet ash twin a ring of such towers, one per planet, connects the whole system to a single place, and the player uses them as the nomai did. the physics is in the records of the high energy lab on ember twin. reviewing the station's logs, pye reports that nomai are arriving at the receiver on brittle hollow

title: Passengers' Avalon
hook: A starliner at half the speed of light on a 120-year run, with hibernation for the passengers, a message home that takes nineteen years, and no relativity.
text: the drive as depicted passengers (sony, 21 december 2016; directed by morten tyldum, written by jon spaihts) states its numbers on screen. the avalon is "the homestead company's premier interstellar starliner" bound for homestead ii; the ship's computer tells jim preston "there are 5,000 passengers and 258 crew members"; the welcome hologram tells him he has spent 120 years in suspended animation, which is the planned duration (transcript). in the observatory he learns the ship left earth "approximately 30 years ago" and "we will arrive in approximately 90 years" . the speed is stated once, by the deck chief gus after he too wakes: "no, we're doing 50% of light speed." . the bartender android arthur states the ship's one rule: "hibernation pods are fail-safe. they never malfunction." . the cause of jim's waking is a meteor strike thirty years in, and someone protests that "the ship's supposed to be meteor-proof" . the ship spins for gravity, carries a fusion reactor that must be vented by hand in the climax, and swings past the star arcturus on the way . the one physics scene is the message. jim records a distress call to the homestead company and the booth answers: "message will arrive in 19 years." and then "earliest reply in 55 years." . those are the film's only statements of a signal limit, and they are honest: light-speed messages, a reply that cannot come in time. origin and lineage spaihts's screenplay was on the 2007 black list; the 2007 draft that circulates online

title: Revelation Space lighthuggers
hook: Reynolds's universe refuses faster-than-light travel outright, runs its plots on decades of light-lag and, when a character tries to break the rule, erases her crew from history.
text: the drive as depicted the ships are lighthuggers. reynolds's own glossary for the series defines one in a sentence: "lighthugger: any large space vehicle with a relativistic cruise ceiling." . his site adds that they "can get very close to the speed of light without ever exceeding it" . they are driven by conjoiner drives, kilometres long, and crewed by ultras who spend the voyages in reefersleep, the series' cryogenic freezing, and who are long-lived partly because of the time dilation of near-light travel . the series timeline places the first relativistic starship's launch from mars orbit in 2205 . the fan wiki's figure of a one-gravity burn to about 99 percent of c in a year is not sourced to any novel and is recorded here as reconstruction . every plot in the sequence (revelation space, 2000; chasm city, 2001; redemption ark, 2002; absolution gap, 2003; galactic north, 2006; inhibitor phase, 2021) is shaped by the fact that crossing between systems costs years of world-time and that news arrives at light speed . the instalment that defines the rule by breaking it is redemption ark (gollancz, 27 june 2002). racing clavain to the cache weapons at resurgam, the conjoiner skade pushes her prototype lighthugger nightshade with inertia-suppressing machinery obtained through the exordium, and attempts a jump to the machinery's "state four", a transition of the matter inside the field from tardyonic to tachyonic, that is, from slower than light to faster . the attempt cripples

title: The Skylark of Space (E. E. Smith, 1928)
hook: The first spaceship in fiction to outrun light by simply pushing harder, in a novel that hears about Einstein's theory and files it under theories.
text: the drive as depicted the skylark is a steel sphere driven by intra-atomic energy released from copper by a catalytic metal the chemist richard seaton calls "x", with a current passed through it; the discovery is made by accident in chapter i, "the occurrence of the impossible" . the power plant is a copper bar mounted in the centre of the ship. the bar pushes the ship along the line of its axis, the ship accelerates for as long as copper lasts, and there is no other mechanism: no field, no bubble, no jump. everything the book says about speed follows from that. the novel is aware of the light barrier and says so before the ship is built. in chapter vii seaton tells the lawyer crane's party that with a four-hundred-pound bar the ship could develop "not only the velocity of light, but an acceleration equal to that velocity", except for "the increase in mass at high velocities, as shown by einstein and others", and that in open space the ship can reach any speed up to light as a limit . two chapters later the limit is gone. duquesne's stolen ship has covered three hundred and fifty million miles in twenty minutes, seaton objects that nothing can go that fast and asks about einstein's theory, and crane answers that a theory is a theory and a measured distance is a fact (chapter viii). the exchange is the whole of the book's physics of faster-than-light travel. from then on the skylark crosses interstellar space at a velocity the narration compares to a rifle bullet against a

title: Spaceballs: ludicrous speed (1987)
hook: Light speed is too slow, so Spaceball One goes to ludicrous speed, turns plaid and overshoots the heroes by a week and a half; the drive is the punchline and knows it.
text: the drive as depicted spaceballs is mel brooks's 1987 parody of star wars and, in passing, of star trek, alien and planet of the apes. its faster-than-light scene is the chase in the first act. lone starr's winnebago, the eagle 5, escapes on its secret hyperjets; aboard the pursuing spaceball one, dark helmet orders light speed, decides "light speed is too slow" and calls for ludicrous speed, and colonel sandurz protests that they have never gone that fast before . the ship's speed dial runs from light speed through ridiculous speed to ludicrous speed. spaceball one streaks past the heroes trailing a tartan wake, and barf, watching it go, delivers the line: "they've gone to plaid" . helmet, pinned in his chair, announces that his brains are going into his feet; sandurz pulls a lever marked as an emergency stop that is never to be used, and helmet is thrown into a console . back on the eagle 5, barf works out what has happened: the spaceballs must have overshot them by a week and a half . that is the entire physics of the drive: three named speeds, one of them absurd; a visual gag in which the star wars hyperspace streak becomes a scottish textile; a joke about acceleration and the human body; a joke about brakes; and a joke that measures distance in time. the film returns to speed once more when spaceball one combs the desert at walking pace, and never again. origin and lineage written by mel brooks, thomas meehan and ronny graham and released by mgm in june 1987 .

title: Star Citizen: quantum drive and jump points
hook: A sublight warp bubble for getting around a system and natural wormholes for getting out of it, in a game that has been in development since 2012 and opened its first jump point to players in 2024.
text: the drive as depicted star citizen (cloud imperium games, directed by chris roberts, crowdfunded from 2012 and playable as an evolving alpha) separates its travel into two mechanisms and keeps them separate in play. within a star system a ship uses its quantum drive: the pilot selects a destination, the drive spools and calibrates, and the ship travels there at very high speed over minutes, with the starfield streaking past and a real transit that can be interrupted . between systems a ship must find a jump point, a natural anomaly at a fixed place near the edge of a system, and fly through a tunnel to the paired point in another system; since alpha 4.0 (december 2024) the first such point, between the stanton and pyro systems, has been open to players, with more added since . the quantum drive is the part with physics. roberts's account, given to the player community, is that the drive makes a bubble around the ship that contracts space ahead and expands it behind, "somewhat inspired by the theory behind an alcubierre drive"; quantum fuel is converted into the negative energy density that shapes the bubble, at a cost in power and heat that larger ships absorb better (chris roberts on the spectrum forum, as transcribed by the star citizen wiki). the in-fiction speed is the point: the drive is sublight. the lore timeline has the first self-sustaining quantum drive built in 2075 at one per cent of light speed and a 2214 engine reaching ten per cent, and the drive's ceiling in

title: Star Trek subspace radio
hook: Starfleet's faster-than-light telephone: a signal through "subspace" at a finite speed with a range limit and relay stations, and a tachyon for every occasion.
text: the drive as depicted subspace radio is in the original series from its first weeks. "the man trap" has spock correcting a "sub-space log"; "charlie x" has uhura "receiving a message on subspace frequency three"; "mudd's women" has a "subspace radio marriage"; "balance of terror" has the romulan treaty "set by sub-space radio" (episode transcripts). what subspace is, the franchise never says on screen; memory alpha's own summary is that "exactly what subspace is has never been revealed on screen", and the one gloss is la forge's honeycomb of infinite cells in "schisms" . the rule that makes it a physics rather than a convenience is that it is finite. in "where no one has gone before" (tng, 1987), flung 2.7 million light years, data reports that the message to starfleet, "traveling subspace, they should receive in fifty-one years, ten months" . that is about 52,000 c, the only number the franchise gives on screen . voyager runs a whole series on the consequence: seventy thousand light years from home, the ship cannot call starfleet at all. in "the 37's" kim dismisses ordinary radio waves, which "only travel at the speed of light. too slow for interstellar communications." . in "message in a bottle" (1998) seven finds "a large network of relay stations. they're alien in origin, abandoned but still functioning", and janeway sends the doctor across "thousands of light years" through it . in "pathfinder" (1999) barclay's midas array, the mutara interdimensional deep space

title: Star Trek: transwarp, quantum slipstream and the other beyond-warp drives
hook: Everything in Star Trek that goes faster than warp: Borg conduits through transwarp space, the infinite-velocity threshold, the quantum slipstream and the mushroom network, each introduced when the plot needed a faster ship and each retired when it did not.
text: the drive as depicted "transwarp" is a label, not a mechanism; the franchise attaches it to at least four unrelated things, and two further drives do the same job under other names. each is defined in one instalment. the excelsior's transwarp drive. star trek iii: the search for spock (1984) introduces the uss excelsior as the great experiment, a ship with a transwarp drive that is meant to outrun the enterprise and fails to engage because scott has sabotaged it . nothing is said about how it would have worked; the film later treats the excelsior as an ordinary warp ship. borg transwarp conduits. "descent" (the next generation, 1993) has a borg ship open a conduit and the enterprise-d follow it; la forge likens the entry to falling into a fast river and being swept along, and computes from the distance covered that the conduit was about twenty times faster than warp 9.8 . "dark frontier" (voyager, 1999) makes the conduits infrastructure: a transwarp coil taken from a borg sphere lets voyager open a conduit and cross twenty thousand light years in days . "endgame" (voyager, 2001) shows the network's hub, a nebula-hidden structure whose conduits reach every quadrant; voyager rides one thirty thousand light years to earth in minutes while the hub is destroyed behind it . later series reuse the abandoned conduits as shortcuts (picard, discovery). the transwarp threshold. title: Star Trek: warp drive (1966 onward)
hook: A subspace field carries the ship at speeds numbered by warp factor on a scale that runs to infinity at warp 10; the drive that gave the physics its name.
text: the drive as depicted star trek never defines its drive in a single scene; it defines it by six decades of consistent usage, one reference book that the production treated as canon in most respects, and a handful of episodes that state rules. the first pilot, "the cage" (1964, aired within "the menagerie" in 1966), speaks of time warp factor and hyperdrive; by the series proper the terms are warp drive and warp factor, with warp 1 as the speed of light and higher factors as faster (memory alpha, sourced to the episodes). the ship is enclosed in a warp field generated by coils in its nacelles, fed by the plasma of a matter-antimatter reaction regulated by dilithium; the field is a distortion of subspace, a domain underlying normal space that star trek uses for both propulsion and communication, and the ship rides the distortion rather than accelerating through space for the on-screen usage, for the technical manual's account. star trek: first contact (1996) shows the first flight: zefram cochrane's phoenix, a converted titan ii missile, breaks the warp barrier on 5 april 2063 and its cockpit display reads space warp generator . an enterprise hallucination in "doctor's orders" gives the plainest on-screen description, that the engine was designed to manipulate space and violate the laws of motion . the scale is the drive's most articulated rule. the original series used a cubic scale, warp factor cubed times c, laid down in the writers' guide and reported in whitfield's the

title: Star Wars: hyperspace (1977 onward)
hook: The hyperdrive that made "jump to lightspeed" a household phrase: a separate dimension entered at speed, navigated by charted lanes and never priced.
text: the drive as depicted the drive is defined in the first film, star wars (1977, later a new hope), in the millennium falcon's escape from tatooine. han solo tells luke they will be safe once they make the jump to hyperspace, then spends the next minute at the navicomputer while the ship is shot at, because the jump needs calculations first: without them the ship could "fly right through a star or bounce too close to a supernova" (shooting script, falcon cockpit scene; the spoken line has "ain't" for the script's "isn't"). two things are fixed here for the whole franchise. hyperspace is somewhere else, entered by a jump and left by a drop. and the danger in it is ordinary matter: stars and other masses on the route, which a good route avoids. the film adds the arrival rule when the falcon drops out at alderaan's coordinates into an asteroid field, han insisting "our position is correct" while the planet is missing . the jump delivers you to the coordinates you computed, whatever is there now. the same film contains the boast that the falcon "made the kessel run in less than twelve parsecs" (cantina scene). a parsec is a unit of distance, about 3.26 light years, so a run measured in parsecs is a route length, not a time. solo: a star wars story (2018) takes the boast literally and builds a set piece on it: the kessel run is a smuggling route through a region of cloud and debris called the maelstrom, around a gravity well called the maw; the standard route is stated in the film

title: Starfield (2023): the grav drive
hook: A ship component with a jump range in light years, a fuel gauge in helium-3 and a backstory in which testing it stripped the Earth of its magnetosphere.
text: the drive as depicted starfield (bethesda game studios, directed by todd howard, released september 2023) is set in 2330 in the settled systems, a region of roughly a hundred star systems within about fifty light years of sol. every ship the player flies has a grav drive, and every trip between systems is a "grav jump": the player picks a destination on the star map, the drive spools for a few seconds while the ship is vulnerable, a distortion spreads from the hull and the ship is gone, arriving at the destination system with no transit shown . the drive is a swappable module with numbers. its "grav jump thrust" sets the maximum jump in light years, reduced by the mass of the ship it is bolted to; no drive in the game exceeds thirty light years in a single jump, so longer trips are chains of jumps through intermediate systems; and each jump burns helium-3 fuel in proportion to distance . the drive also supplies the ship's artificial gravity, so a ship with its grav drive powered down floats . the in-game name is the graviton loop array; a longer name, graviton loop field array, was given by howard in interview . nothing in the game states what the drive does to space. the visual is a bending of the starfield around the ship and a flash; the word is "grav"; that is all. the lore does something else. in the main quest "unearthed" the player enters the ruined nasa launch tower on earth and reads dr victor aiza's terminals: an artefact recovered from mars, a prototype drive

title: Stargate: the gate network (1994 film, SG-1 1997 onward)
hook: A ring that dials another ring: stable wormholes between fixed gates, one way for matter, thirty-eight minutes at a time, built by somebody long gone.
text: the drive as depicted the 1994 film (directed by roland emmerich, written by emmerich and dean devlin, released 28 october 1994) defines the device . a ring excavated at giza carries thirty-nine symbols; the linguist daniel jackson works out that an address is six constellations fixing a point in space plus a seventh symbol for the point of origin, and when seven chevrons lock the ring opens a wormhole to a matching ring on a desert planet . in the film that planet lies in another galaxy, the kaliam galaxy, millions of light years away; the television series later moved it into the milky way . the opening of the gate is a burst of what the production called the kawoosh, a water-vortex effect filmed in a glass tube, after which the event horizon settles into a standing pool that travellers step into . the film's own account of transit is that matter entering the event horizon is broken down and sent through the wormhole, then reconstituted at the far gate . stargate sg-1 (1997 to 2007), atlantis (2004 to 2009) and universe (2009 to 2011) added the rules, and each rule has an episode. the pilot "children of the gods" establishes that matter travels one way, from the dialling gate to the receiving gate, while radio signals pass in both directions . the thirty-eight-minute limit, after which a wormhole closes on its own unless enormous power is supplied, is stated in the sg-1 episode "a matter of time" and is the title of the atlantis episode "thirty-eight minutes" . title: Stargate: the ships' hyperdrives
hook: The starships of SG-1 and Atlantis open a window into hyperspace and cross galaxies at speeds set by whose engine is fitted; a tiered technology, distinct from the gates, that the franchise rations by power source.
text: the drive as depicted the stargate franchise has two ways between the stars, and this dossier is about the second. the gates, stable wormholes between fixed rings, have their own dossier in the l3 catalogue. ships have hyperdrives, and the hyperdrive is shown long before it is explained. a goa'uld ha'tak mothership carries sg-1 from chulak toward earth in the first-season finale "within the serpent's grasp" (1998), the ship entering and leaving hyperspace through a bright window that opens ahead of it . from then on every spacefaring power in the series has a hyperdrive, and the drama is in whose is faster. the rules are stated by incident rather than by lecture. in "enemies" (season 5, episode 1, 29 june 2001) sg-1's captured ha'tak is thrown into another galaxy by the shock of a supernova its crew had set off; the franchise wiki places it four million light-years out with a return time of a hundred and twenty-five years at top speed, and the episode's resolution is that replicators aboard modify the engines so the ship exceeds its fastest velocity by eight hundred times, making the trip home short (the episode's own plot; the distance and time figures are the wiki's ). earth's first hyperdrive ship, the x-303 prometheus, is introduced in "prometheus" (season 6, episode 11, 23 august 2002) with a naquadria-powered hyperdrive that earth's engineers cannot make work until a goa'uld's knowledge corrects the error; hijacked, the ship jumps and emerges twelve hundred light-years

title: Starman Jones: the congruencies (Heinlein 1953)
hook: Space folded back on itself at charted points that must be hit exactly, with the tables done by hand; get the arithmetic wrong and the ship is nowhere.
text: the drive as depicted robert a. heinlein's starman jones (charles scribner's sons, 1953) is a novel about the astrogators' guild, and its drive is whatever the astrogators compute . the starship asgard travels between stars by passing through anomalies, points in space where, as the text has it, space is folded back on itself so that a long distance becomes no distance; a ship that reaches the anomaly on exactly the right course and speed makes a transition and is instantly elsewhere, at the congruent point near the destination . the novel gives the geometry a rule: "anomalies are always flat, otherwise they couldn't fit together", which is to say the two ends must be congruent surfaces for the fold to join them (quoted on the mathfiction database from the text; not verified against a copy for this dossier). reference summaries call the anomalies horst congruencies and the drive the horst-conrad; this catalogue has not confirmed the names against the text . space is curved near stars and planets and nearly flat between them, so the anomalies lie in flat regions, and a ship must reach them by ordinary flight and hit them at the computed speed . the whole story is in the computing. the ship's computer is a calculator with no readable output; astrogators enter figures and read results through printed tables, converting decimal to binary and back, and an astrogator's competence is the speed and accuracy with which he does this under time pressure as the ship approaches an

title: Stellaris: warp, hyperlane and wormhole (Paradox Development Studio, 2016)
hook: A strategy game that offered its players a choice of loophole at the start, one each from L2, L4 and L3, and then in 2018 took two of them away.
text: the drive as depicted stellaris at release (version 1.0, may 2016) made faster-than-light travel a choice each empire fixed at creation, and the game's dev diary #4, "means of travel" (october 2015), is the designers' own definition of the three options (developer statement; the moddb repost dated april 2016 was the copy read). warp needs a warp drive on every ship, costly and power-hungry, and allows travel to any system within range in any direction; a journey beyond range is a sequence of jumps, each of which strains the drive and imposes a cooldown; fleets must jump from the edge of a system "to lessen the gravitational pull of the local star", and warp is the slowest of the three, so an arriving fleet's entry point is predictable and can be ambushed . wormhole travel dispenses with the drive: a wormhole station on the edge of a system opens a temporary wormhole through which a fleet is moved instantly to a distant system; the station generates one wormhole at a time, a larger fleet takes longer to prepare, the wormhole allows two-way travel and collapses almost at once, and an empire's reach is its network of stations, which can be disabled by raiders . hyperdrive uses a hidden network of hyperlanes connecting systems, visible only to those who can see it, along which ships travel fast but only along the lanes; voids without systems block movement, lane junctions are chokepoints, and because the lanes exist in subspace a fleet can enter one from anywhere in a system

title: Tau Zero's ramjet
hook: Anderson's Bussard ramjet loses its brakes, and the crew ride time dilation past the end of the universe rather than around the light barrier.
text: the drive as depicted the leonora christine is an interstellar ramjet carrying twenty-five men and twenty-five women from earth to beta virginis, about thirty light years away, on a flight planned to take five years by ship time and thirty-three by earth's . the ship scoops interstellar hydrogen, fuses it and throws it back; the same fields that gather fuel shield the crew from the hydrogen they are hitting . the novel names its physics in its title. tau is the time-contraction factor, the reciprocal of the lorentz factor, and anderson defines it in the narration as the square root of one minus the square of the ship's speed over the speed of light; the closer the speed comes to light's, the closer tau comes to zero (formula as given by wikipedia and by a physics-journal treatment; the chapter was not identified). the mission's planned peak is tau of about 0.015 . the prose is narrative "interspersed with paragraphs" in which anderson explains relativity and the ship's mechanics, and a chapter-13 image of "two globes, fiery blue ahead, deep crimson aft" is the doppler shift of the sky seen from the bridge . the accident defines the book. before the halfway point the ship passes through a small nebula that damages the deceleration field generators . the drive cannot be shut down for repairs, because the ram fields are also the radiation shielding and the engines' own radiation makes the damaged section unapproachable, so the ship can neither stop accelerating nor be fixed .

title: The Orville: quantum drive (2017 onward)
hook: A ship whose three rings fold space into a bubble that crosses ten light years an hour, designed by a science consultant who says out loud that it is an Alcubierre drive.
text: the drive as depicted the uss orville travels at quantum speed using a quantum drive, and the show's characters talk about it the way star trek's talk about warp: as a setting, a speed and a thing that can break. two episodes define it. in "pria" (season 1, episode 5, 2017) captain mercer states the ship's speed as in excess of ten light years per hour ; in "new dimensions" (1x11, 2017) the engineer john lamarr says the drive creates "quantum bubbles" that the ship travels in, and the plot turns on a two-dimensional region of space that would knock the quantum engine out of alignment . the third-season episode "from unknown graves" (3x07, 2022) upgrades the ship to a fourth-generation engine rated at seventeen light years an hour . the drive is fuelled by dysonium, stored in tanks behind containment regulators and processed before injection into the engines; "firestorm" (1x10) makes containment a plot point . the ship's three rings are the engine: each ring carries a quantum engine and the rings are the visual signature of union ships. that is all the show says on screen. it does not name alcubierre, negative energy, exotic matter or a metric, and the physics content in this dossier's next section comes from the production, not the episodes. origin and lineage the orville was created by seth macfarlane and premiered on fox on 10 september 2017; the third season moved to hulu in 2022 . its science consultant and supervising producer andré bormanis, who had held the same role

title: Thor (2011): the Bifrost
hook: Asgard's rainbow bridge, named on screen as an Einstein–Rosen bridge, opened and closed by a gatekeeper and shattered by its own god to keep it from being used as a weapon.

title: Death's End: curvature propulsion (Liu Cixin, 2010)
hook: Ships that flatten the space behind them and are pulled forward to lightspeed, never past it, leaving trails in which light itself is slowed; the one great space opera that refuses FTL and builds its ending on the refusal.

title: Time for the Stars' telepathy
hook: Heinlein's twins talk across light years in the same instant, the torchship pays for it in the twin paradox, and the book ends by turning the loophole into a drive.
text: the drive as depicted time for the stars (scribner's, august 1956) is narrated by tom bartlett, one of a pair of identical twins recruited by the long range foundation because some twins can talk to each other by telepathy, and telepathy has been measured to be faster than light . the measurement is given in chapter ii: a twin sent to ganymede while the other stayed in buenos aires, with simultaneous radio and telepathic messages, and "the telepathic message always beat the radio message by about forty minutes."; the signal was as strong at half a billion miles as at home and "doesn't pay attention to the inverse-square law either" . tom ships out on the torchship lewis and clark, the "elsie", a mass-converter vessel whose torch "spits the mass out as radiation at the speed of light", boosting at 124 percent of a gravity to reach about five percent of c in two weeks and "the better part of a year" to approach light speed (chs. vi, viii, xiii). the twins are the ship's radio. chapter viii, "relativity", is where the book argues with physics. dr babcock, the ship's relativist, has the twins tick against a metronome to measure the lag of the link with sound-speed and feedback delays removed, and says the aim is to find out what the word "simultaneous" means; since einstein, "'simultaneous' and 'simultaneity' have been dirty words to physicists", "we chucked the very concept, denied that it had meaning", and then the mind readers came along and kicked it over . o'toole's result

title: Timescape's tachyon message
hook: A working physicist's novel in which a 1998 laboratory beams a warning to 1962 by tachyon, and the paradox is handled with the same care as the apparatus.

title: Vinge's Zones of Thought: FTL only where physics permits it (1992)
hook: The one setting in which the laws governing faster-than-light travel change with where you are: no FTL near the galactic core, an ultradrive out toward the rim, and the boundary as a wall you can be stranded behind.

title: Warhammer 40,000: the Warp (1987 onward)
hook: A second reality made of emotion and inhabited by things that want in, crossed behind a Gellar field, steered by a mutant who can see it, with time that does not agree with ours.
text: the drive as depicted the setting began as the tabletop rulebook warhammer 40,000: rogue trader (games workshop, 1987), and has been restated in ten further rulebook editions to 2026, in army codexes, in the battlefleet gothic fleet game (1999), in hundreds of black library novels and in licensed video games (wikipedia, "warhammer 40,000", edition list). the drive is therefore defined by the rulebook background rather than by any one story. the elements are stable across editions. the warp, also called the immaterium or the empyrean, is a parallel dimension of psychic energy, formed and stirred by the emotions of every mind in the material universe and home to the chaos gods and their daemons (wikipedia, "warhammer 40,000", setting). a warp drive tears a hole into it; the ship travels in it, carried by its currents, and drops back into real space having crossed a distance that would take centuries at sublight (rulebook background, from memory across editions; no rulebook page could be opened this session). three rules govern the crossing. a gellar field, a projected bubble of real-space conditions around the hull, keeps the warp and its inhabitants out; a failed field means the crew are taken (from memory; the lexicanum and fandom articles could not be opened). a navigator, a member of a mutant human bloodline with a third eye that perceives the warp, steers by the light of the astronomican, a psychic beacon projected from terra by the emperor's mind; without a navigator a

title: Wing Commander (1990) and the 1999 film: jump points
hook: A war fought around fixed jump points between star systems, told first as a carrier pilot's briefings and then, in the film, as a story about the people who can feel where the points are.
text: the drive as depicted wing commander (origin systems, 1990, designed by chris roberts) is a space combat game in which the player flies fighters from the carrier tiger's claw in a war between the terran confederation and the kilrathi. its faster-than-light travel is never flown by the player. star systems are connected by jump points, fixed places where a ship with a jump drive can leave one system and appear in another; the game's mission briefings treat them as terrain, positions to defend, patrol or mine, and the carrier's movement between systems is a jump the player is told about, not shown . the manual, written by aaron allston as an issue of the in-fiction magazine claw marks, uses the vocabulary without explaining it: mission types include guarding a stationary position such as a capital ship, a base or a jump point; a history of the enyo engagement has the confederation mine a system's principal jump point and bring its fleet through it into the battle; a news item has the committee for interaction with alien intelligences launching "unmanned probes to uncharted jump-spheres" and a probe reappearing "in a terran jump-point" with data from a new species (claw marks, 1990, the mission-types section, the enyo engagement history and the news page). jump-spheres, jump buoys marking known points and the rule that only a properly equipped ship can transit are the whole of the 1990 statement . the later games (1991 to 1997) keep the same picture and add cinematic jump

title: Campbell's Islands of Space (1931): where the word came from
hook: The first use of "hyperspace" for a way to beat light, and the thing it named was not a separate space but a bubble of altered space around the ship.
text: the drive as depicted islands of space is the second of john w. campbell's arcot, wade and morey novels, published in the spring 1931 amazing stories quarterly and revised for the fantasy press book of 1957 (wikipedia, "islands of space", publication history). the text read for this dossier is the project gutenberg copy, which is the revised book text, so what follows describes the drive as campbell left it in 1957; the one sentence certainly from 1931 is the dictionary citation, "in the hyperspace we are going into, a new condition exists" (historical dictionary of science fiction, entry "hyperspace", citing campbell 1931). the drive is defined in two conversations. in chapter 1 arcot explains that the velocity of light is a property of space and that light slows in water because the fields between atoms increase the curvature of the space there; reverse that, "by changing the curvature of the space surrounding you", and any velocity is available, instantaneously and without felt acceleration, because every particle of the ship is moved alike (revised text, chapter 1). in chapter 5 the machinery is shown: a large storage coil that, instead of holding its field inside, affects all the space around it, so that the ship is enclosed in "a hyperspace of our own making" (chapter 5). the word, at its first use for space travel, names a pocket the ship carries, not a place it goes to. the rules follow in the same conversation and are kept for the rest of the book. the crew cannot

title: Xenocide: travel through the Outside
hook: Orson Scott Card's 1991 answer to his own instantaneous ansible: a ship whose every particle is held in one mind is pushed out of the universe and back in somewhere else, and whatever else that mind holds comes back with it.

title: Space Battleship Yamato: warp by wave motion engine
hook: The 1974 anime's rebuilt battleship crosses 148,000 light-years and back inside a year on an engine built from alien plans; the same engine fires the ship's great gun, and every warp is a leap the crew feel.
text: the drive as depicted space battleship yamato (uchū senkan yamato) ran on yomiuri television from 6 october 1974 to 30 march 1975, twenty-six episodes cut down from a planned thirty-nine, produced by yoshinobu nishizaki with leiji matsumoto directing and designing . the premise sets the drive's terms. earth has been bombed radioactive by gamilas; a capsule from queen starsha of iscandar, 148,000 light-years away, offers the cosmo cleaner (cosmo dna in the english dub) that can undo it, and contains the plans for an engine that can "propel a ship at faster-than-light speeds" . humanity has one year before the underground cities fail, and the series counts the days down at the end of every episode . the engine, the wave motion engine (hadō enjin), is built into the raised wreck of the battleship yamato, and the series is the round trip. the first warp is episode 4, "world of wonder! yamato leaps past light!", broadcast 27 october 1974 . the ship, having reached the moon under ordinary thrust, must time the warp precisely, and the bridge crew count it in; the episode shows the warp as a passage between the third dimension and the fourth, with the ship stretching and the stars streaming, during which the crew see visions and the ship's clocks and the crew's sense of time slip . the ship emerges where the calculation said it would, the bridge confirms the jump against the charts, and the next episode opens at jupiter . later warps carry the ship further per jump, and the dialogue

title: Feinberg's tachyon, outward
hook: Feinberg names the faster-than-light particle in 1967, having been set thinking by a 1954 story; the word then goes back into fiction, carrying its physics exactly once (Timescape) and travelling everywhere else as a stock word for faster than light.

title: Hyperspace: the word
hook: A mathematician's word for space with more than three dimensions (recorded from 1852) is borrowed by a pulp writer in 1928, made into a drive by Campbell in 1931, passed down the magazine he came to edit and made universal by Star Wars in 1977, while the physics it sounds like never meant any of it.
text: the line the word came first and the idea came later. "hyperspace" was a term of nineteenth-century geometry for a space of more than three dimensions, and the oxford english dictionary's third edition dates that sense to 1852 (as reported in the etymology note of the historical dictionary of science fiction; the oed itself is behind a paywall and was not opened). it is the same sense the physics of extra dimensions still uses, which is why the physics end of this line is kaluza-klein and the hyperspace reading: kaluza's fifth dimension (1921) and klein's compact circle (1926) are hyperspace in the 1852 meaning, more directions on the same manifold, and nothing else. the fiction sense, a separate region with its own rules that a ship can enter and leave, has no counterpart there, which is what the register's man-1 says. the fiction sense grew in two steps. kirk meadowcroft's "the invisible bubble" (amazing stories, september 1928) used "hyper-space" as a place next door to ours, with "boundary lines" that "may not be so rigidly drawn as we have supposed", but nobody travels by it (historical dictionary of science fiction, entry "hyperspace", first two citations). three years later john w. campbell's islands of space (amazing stories quarterly, spring 1931) attached the word to a way of beating light, and that is the first such use the dictionary can find . the catalogue's dossier on that text, campbell 1931, records the twist: campbell's ship does not go anywhere. its main

title: Le Guin's ansible goes out into the field
hook: One invented word for instant messaging between stars, coined in 1966, given its theory in 1974 and then lent, with its author's blessing, to half of science fiction.
text: the line ursula k. le guin's first novel, rocannon's world (ace, 1966), has a league ethnologist on a lost planet with a box that talks to league headquarters across interstellar distance without delay. the box is called an ansible, and the estate's own page for the novel records that this is the word's first appearance. le guin's ansible is the dossier for the device and for what she did with it eight years later in the dispossessed (1974), where the physicist shevek works out the theory of simultaneity that makes it buildable and gives it away to everybody. so the word came first and the invention came second, in the same author's hands, which is the reverse of the usual order. where the word itself came from is the one thing le guin never wrote down. the account that she clipped it from "answerable" survives only because dave goldman asked her and reported the answer on usenet in april 2001, and the dictionaries have taken his word for it. the borrowings are documented better than the coinage. orson scott card used the word in "ender's game" (analog, august 1977) and in the 1985 novel, whose text says the name was dredged out of an old book; on his own site he wrote that the word "originated with ursula k. leguin" and that he used it "for the same reason that we all use 'robot' and 'waldo'", while the philotic mechanism was his own. that mechanism is ender's philotic ansible, and its extension into a starship, xenocide's outside, is card's alone; asked in 1999 whether

title: The wormhole goes to television
hook: After 1988 the word "wormhole" turned up wherever a series needed a door between stars; how much of that was the paper and how much was the word already being in the air is the question this page asks.
text: the line before morris and thorne 1988 the wormhole was a physicist's word for something nothing could cross. wheeler coined it in 1957 for the schwarzschild bridge, and fuller and wheeler showed in 1962 that the bridge pinches shut before a signal gets through. television used the word anyway: star trek: the motion picture (1979) throws the enterprise into a "wormhole" caused by a warp imbalance, and isaac asimov, consulted on the film, objected to the word and proposed "temporal tunnel". bujold's vorkosigan books were routing ships through wormholes from 1986. so the word did not need the paper. what the paper added was the adjective. morris and thorne made a wormhole that stays open, and within eighteen months star trek: the next generation had "the price" (13 november 1989), an episode built around a stable wormhole, the first of its kind. four years after that deep space nine opened on one: in "emissary" (3 january 1993) dax announces "the first stable wormhole known to exist", and the series parks its station at the mouth for seven years. there is no dossier for the bajoran wormhole in this catalogue, and the absence is recorded below. the stargate film of 1994 is the odd one out: its gate is a "doorway between our worlds" and the transcript never says wormhole. the word arrives with the series. in "children of the gods" (1997) carter says the energy needed to "create a stable wormhole" is astronomical and points at the fluctuations in the event horizon, and from then

title: Physicists in the writers' room
hook: The documented cases of a working scientist designing or naming a fictional drive, from Dan Alderson's tramlines in 1974 to Kip Thorne's wormhole in 2014, and which of them produced physics rather than vocabulary.
text: the line this page cuts across the others. most lineage in the catalogue is a word or a picture travelling on its own; here the carrier is a person with a physics degree who was asked to make a drive for a story. the first well-documented case is dan alderson of the jet propulsion laboratory, whose friends larry niven and jerry pournelle handed him a list of what their interstellar drive should allow and forbid and let him design one to the specification. the result is the alderson drive of the mote in god's eye (1974), named for its designer, and the account is the authors' own, in the essay "building the mote in god's eye" (galaxy, january 1976). the essay has not been read for this catalogue; its story reaches us through atomic rockets and the reference wikis, and is graded as such. the second case is the one with a paper attached. in the summer of 1985 carl sagan sent kip thorne a draft of contact and asked for help with the gravity; thorne and his student michael morris found the traversable wormhole solutions, sagan put them into the novel at galley proof, and the physicists wrote it all up in morris and thorne 1988, whose section i.c says so in as many words. that single request produced the contact machine, a k4 entry on the register and, twenty-six years on, the interstellar wormhole, for which thorne served as executive producer and consultant and with the visual effects team published the geometry in the american journal of physics in 2015. that line has its own

title: Sagan asks Thorne for a legal wormhole
hook: A novelist's request in 1985 produced the traversable wormhole paper and the paper produced a time machine; the same physicist and producer then carried the wormhole into Interstellar three decades later.
text: the line this is the one line in the catalogue that runs from fiction into physics and back out again, and the paper at its centre says so in its own text. in the summer of 1985 carl sagan sent kip thorne a prepublication draft of contact and asked for help making its gravitational physics as accurate as possible. thorne and his student michael morris looked for a wormhole that a person could actually cross, found the class of solutions now named after them and sent sagan a preliminary description; sagan wrote the results into the novel at the galley proof stage, and the book came out that september. the paper itself, morris and thorne 1988, appeared in the american journal of physics three years later, opens its abstract by naming the novel and thanks sagan in its acknowledgements. what travelled from sagan to thorne was a question: is there any way through? what travelled back was a metric with a bill attached, matter with negative energy density at the throat, which sagan paid by giving the tunnels to a vanished civilisation. the paper had a sequel within months. thinking about what a traversable wormhole could do, morris, thorne and yurtsever showed that moving one mouth on a fast round trip turns the shortcut into a time machine, the morris, thorne and yurtsever time machine of physical review letters, and that a wormhole needs the averaged energy condition to fail. thorne's own account of the whole episode, from sagan's request to the time machine, is the final chapter

title: Star Trek to Alcubierre and back out
hook: A television drive of 1966 lends its name to a general relativity paper in 1994, and the paper then lends its name and its bill back to three fictions that name the physicist.
text: the line the word came first. star trek premiered on nbc on 8 september 1966 with a ship that moved by warp drive, and the catalogue's star trek warp drive dossier records that the word itself is older still, going back to john w. campbell's islands of space (1931), which is the story told on hyperspace-the-word. for twenty-eight years the drive was a stage convention with a warp factor chart and no physics. then miguel alcubierre, a doctoral student at cardiff, published a four-page letter in classical and quantum gravity showing that general relativity permits a bubble of spacetime to carry a ship faster than light as seen from outside, at the price of negative energy. the abstract of alcubierre 1994 says the distortion is "reminiscent of the 'warp drive' of science fiction". that sentence is the whole of the primary evidence for the borrowing, and it names science fiction, not star trek. star trek by name rests on alcubierre's later interviews, and until this page was written the catalogue had found none of them. there is now one in his own voice. in a long bbva "aprendemos juntos" conversation, posted to youtube in december 2024, alcubierre says that as a child he watched everything in science fiction and a lot of viaje a las estrellas, that in those programmes the ships always go faster than light, and that the idea of cheating relativity came to him during his doctorate while he was studying black holes. that is a weaker claim than the popular one. the show gave him

title: The paper fold
hook: Mark two points on a sheet, fold it so they touch, push a pen through: the one demonstration of a shortcut that every audience has seen, traced from a folded scarf in 1953 to a film that names its own sources.

title: Tolman's paradox to Timescape
hook: Einstein notices in 1907 that a faster-than-light signal would let an effect precede its cause; Tolman restates it in 1917; Benford, Book and Newcomb name it the antitelephone in 1970; Benford then spends ten years turning his own paper into a novel.
text: the line the paradox is older than the particle. in §5 of his 1907 review for the jahrbuch der radioaktivität und elektronik einstein used the addition theorem for velocities to show that if a signal travelled at w > c "one can always choose v such that t < 0", so that "the achieved effect would precede the cause"; he found no logical contradiction in this but held that it "conflicts with the character of all our experience" enough to prove w > c impossible (einstein 1907, pp. 423–424, quoted in weinstein 2012; the einstein papers site redirected to a portal announcement on 2026-09-13, and the register's cau-1 carries the page reference as verified). richard tolman put the same argument into his 1917 textbook the theory of the relativity of motion, §52, "velocities greater than that of light", pp. 54–55: an impulse from a to b at speed u and a second frame moving at v; for uv/c² above one "the effect which occurs at b would precede in time its cause" (read in the archive.org scan). tolman does not cite the 1907 paper in that section (his one jahrbuch reference is to a 1910 volume), so the link from einstein to tolman is one of content, which the historians of the subject treat as plain (kragh's 2025 history of pre-feinberg tachyons calls tolman's version "almost identical to einstein's"). by 1923 the idea was public property: the punch limerick about the young lady named bright, who "returned on the previous night", is tolman's paradox in five lines (same source; the verse

title: The antitelephone
hook: You stay home. Your friend flies past at a good fraction of light speed. You send a message faster than light; she replies the same way, by her own clock and her own idea of "instant". Here is when the reply lands.
text: the antitelephone you stay home. your friend flies past at a good fraction of light speed. you send a message faster than light; she replies the same way, by her own clock and her own idea of "instant". here is when the reply lands. things to notice faster than light is already backwards in time for someone set the message speed just above c and slide her speed up. in her frame your outbound message tilts until it points into her past, before it ever reaches her. why the tilt the reply is the killer one ftl message is odd but survivable. two, exchanged between people in relative motion, deliver the answer before the question. that is the antitelephone. why two there is a threshold the reply beats the question only when her speed exceeds 2u over 1 plus u squared, with u the message speed in units of c. at ten times light speed, walking pace nearly does it. the formula switching frames changes nothing draw it in her frame instead. same events, same order of cause and effect for anyone on either worldline. the paradox is not an illusion of one viewpoint. what is invariant the one escape is a preferred frame if "instant" meant instant in one special frame for everyone, the reply could never beat the question. that escape costs you special relativity for the ftl sector. register cau-4 every drive in the catalogue owes this bill warp bubbles, wormholes, hyperspace, ansibles: any of them lets you build this diagram. the register scores each on what it does about it. register cau-1

title: The Alcubierre bubble
hook: The ship sits still in a patch of flat space. Space squeezes in front of that patch and stretches behind it, and the patch is carried along faster than light. Here is the bubble from above, the shape of its wall and the bill for building it.
text: the alcubierre bubble the ship sits still in a patch of flat space. space squeezes in front of that patch and stretches behind it, and the patch is carried along faster than light. here is the bubble from above, the shape of its wall and the bill for building it. things to notice watch the grid get carried leave the grid on "carried" and slide the carry distance up. every vertex inside the bubble moves as one block and nothing outside moves at all, so the wall squeezes the lines together ahead and pulls them apart behind. that squeeze and stretch is the expansion view, drawn with particles instead of colour. what the grid is the ship never breaks the speed limit pick the shape view and push the speed to 10c. the flat patch around the ship, where the shape function is 1, does not change at all. only the wall does any work. inside, clocks tick at the home rate and nobody feels any push. why nothing happens inside above c the crew cannot steer slide the speed past 1c and a dashed ring appears in the wall. that ring is a horizon: light sent forward from the ship gets no further. the front of the wall is out of the crew's reach, so the pilot's chair is decorative. register con-1 the route has to be laid in advance keep the speed above 1c and look at the front wall. the stuff that shapes it is ahead of anything the ship can send, so it cannot be put there from the ship. someone has to build the track first, at sublight speed. register con-2 a thicker wall is cheaper, and forbidden
